lines.text: Telling time in English involves more than just reading numbers on a clock. The 12-hour clock is standard in daily conversation, using 'a.m.' (ante meridiem — before noon) and 'p.m.' (post meridiem — after noon). When the minute hand points to 12, it's 'o'clock' — three o'clock, seven o'clock. 'Quarter past' means 15 minutes after the hour, 'half past' means 30 minutes after, and 'quarter to' means 15 minutes before the next hour. For other times, English uses 'past' for the first half of the hour (ten past three = 3:10) and 'to' for the second half (twenty to four = 3:40). The 24-hour clock is used in timetables, military contexts, and formal schedules — fourteen hundred hours (14:00) rather than two p.m. Noon is 12:00 p.m. and midnight is 12:00 a.m., though saying 'noon' and 'midnight' avoids confusion. Time-related vocabulary extends to periods of the day: dawn (sunrise), morning, midday, afternoon, dusk (sunset), evening, and night. Approximate times use phrases like 'around', 'about', 'just after', 'just before', 'nearly', and 'almost'. Understanding how English speakers discuss time — punctuality, scheduling, and time zones — is essential for professional and social communication.

lines.text: In British and American culture, punctuality is highly valued. Being 'on time' means arriving exactly at or slightly before the scheduled time. Being 5 minutes late requires an apology. 'Fashionably late' (10-15 minutes) is acceptable only at social events.
lines.name: In British and American culture, punctuality is highly valued. Being 'on time' means arriving exactly at or slightly before the scheduled time. Being 5 minutes late requires an apology. 'Fashionably late' (10-15 minutes) is acceptable only at social events.

lines.text: Everyday English uses the 12-hour clock with a.m./p.m. The 24-hour clock is called 'military time' in America. In the UK, timetables and official documents use it. '1400 hours' = 2:00 p.m. Digital clocks often default to 24-hour format.

lines.text: English has specific time zone abbreviations: GMT (Greenwich Mean Time), BST (British Summer Time), EST (Eastern Standard Time), PST (Pacific Standard Time). When scheduling international calls, saying 'my time' or 'your time' prevents confusion.

lines.text: 'O'clock' comes from 'of the clock'. 'AM' and 'PM' are Latin: ante meridiem and post meridiem. 'Sharp' means exactly (e.g. 'nine o'clock sharp'). 'Ish' means approximately ('around three-ish'). 'On the dot' = exactly on time.

lines.text: Big Ben (the bell in London's Elizabeth Tower) is a global symbol of timekeeping. Greenwich in London is where the Prime Meridian (0° longitude) runs — the reference point for world time. GMT remains the foundation of global time zones.
